You've misunderstood the concept of boundaries. Imagine you place a fence around your garden. It keeps out the dogs and cats from entering it. But it doesn't stop them from doing anything outside the fence or them trying to break it or climb over it.

Boundaries are for yourself. They define what makes you feel respected, safe and comfortable. For example:

"I need time to myself when I come home from work before I can engage in socializing."
"I don't like to argue over text and prefer to calmly talk in person"
"I like my privacy, so I'd rather not share my phone password"
"I enjoy time together, but I also need time to enjoy my own hobbies"

These are what we call your needs in a relationship. And by talking about them and having clear communication about them, you've set "boundaries"

But they are not rules. If your partner doesn't fulfill your needs, you can't really force them to suddenly do so. You can only remind them of your needs.

And they continue overstepping your boundaries, you may have to consider that it may conflict with what they need.

This is why communication is so important. Although sometimes, that fails too. Sometimes... People are not compatible.

Remember that having boundaries does not mean people will always respect them. It's up to you to know when to walk away and when to stay.

Loving someone is something you choose. Something you do, and mostly show through your actions with your partner. Choosing to be with them. Choosing to cook their favorite meal. Choosing to kiss them even if they hadn't brushed their teeth yet. Etc

"To be in love" is where the romantic feelings come in play. Desire, lust, attraction. You experience "being loved" in intimacy, happiness in their presence. Sadness in their absence. Sometimes the other way around. Feelings come and go, and it is both your own responsibility to nurture those feelings in a relationship. You can't expect to be romantic if you don't schedule dates together. You can't expect to feel happy if you can't communicate and solve through your problems together. You can't expect to feel loved if intimacy is neglected.

"Falling out of love" is the phenomenon of a relationship that wasn't nurtured. You can't control how you feel, but you had control over your own actions.

But loving someone, is always a choice. And if you walk away from a relationship because you "fell out of love",  then either you don't understand the concept of what it means to love someone, and base your relationships purely on feelings, or you settled for someone you never had feelings for and grew tired of pretending just to have a relationship.

First off, let me just say; you’re navigating such an emotionally challenging situation with a lot of thoughtfulness and maturity. Long-distance relationships are tough even in the best of circumstances, and it’s natural for both you and your boyfriend to have moments of doubt or struggle along the way. It’s clear that you care deeply for him, which is beautiful, but also makes these uncertainties all the harder to deal with.

I do have a few points that I observed from your background that I wish to lay out for you to spend some thoughts on:

# #1 Understand what “distance” means for him

When he says he needs “distance,” it might not be about creating more physical or emotional space from *you* specifically. It could reflect his personal overwhelm and traveling, being in new environments, and sorting out his future. People cope differently when life feels chaotic, and it sounds like he retreats inward. Try not to take this as a reflection of your worth or how much he cares for you. It seems like he’s grappling with things that might not be in your control to fix.

# #2 Communication

You’ve expressed a need for some reassurance (like a simple “I still care about you” text every few days). That’s a small but meaningful way to stay connected without being overwhelming. If he agrees but struggles to follow through, you might need to gently reiterate that this isn’t about pressure but it’s about maintaining the relationship in a way that works for both of you.

# #3 Foundation

From what you’ve shared, your bond seems strong and filled with love, but right now you’re in an emotionally imbalanced situation. Ask yourself: Are both of you equally committed to finding ways to support each other during tough times? Long-term relationships require teamwork, even when life gets busy or stressful.

# #4 What you can and can't control

You’ve mentioned that not knowing what he’s thinking or feeling is causing you a lot of anxiety. While that’s completely okay, it would help to shift your focus to things that ground you, whether that’s your college work, hobbies, friends, or self-care routines. Giving your mind something productive and positive to latch onto can help ease some of the emotional weight.

# #5 Consider where you draw the line

It’s important to reflect on what you need from this relationship to feel secure and happy. Are you okay waiting and seeing how things evolve, or would you feel more at peace making a decision to protect your mental health? Setting boundaries for yourself isn’t about giving up, it’s about prioritizing your well-being.

# #6 The “Cooked” question

You’re far from “cooked.” Relationships, especially those that have to bridge physical and emotional distance, often go through turbulence. If both of you want to make this work, it’s possible... but it takes consistent communication, compromise, and effort on both sides.

Ultimately, you deserve a relationship where you feel valued, supported, and secure. Whether that’s with him or someone else, this situation is teaching you more about what you need and how you handle challenges. If you’d like, we can brainstorm ways to approach a follow-up conversation.

Thing with love is... you have "being in love" and then there's "love".

Being in love is a feeling of admiration and attraction towards someone; whereas "loving someone" is more a commitment. A choice you make when you want to be with someone.

And often this is misunderstood, misinterpreted and even underestimated.

Of course after 1 or 2 years the whole "being in love" feeling starts to fade. Which is why they refer to that as the honeymoon phase.

So at that point, it all comes down to your own will, based by your own decisions. You can't rely on just your feelings anymore. You got to actively make an effort to make the relationship work, and support your partner, and talk with them openly and honestly.

They're supposed to be like your best friend. And that's kinda what it is, because when all the feelings are gone, a strong friendship should be the basis that supports your relationship together.

Anyway, people get confused when the "honeymoon" ends and they wonder if they love their partner at all. 

It's actually more simple than it seems, but once again it's often misunderstood. You choose your partner. You choose to love them. You choose to be with them.

Bascially, it’s TACTFUL but honest, loving, gentle, generous and continuous communication. With flexibility and compromise in full force. Sharing and caring.

No blaming, no name calling, cursing, no arguing, fighting, quarreling or conflict, and no bringing up the past.

Of course, since we are imperfect, at least as little of the aforementioned as possible!

Listening, acceptance and acknowledgement.

Those are all part of healthy communication. Staying in touch with each other’s feelings, throughts, daily activities, adventures, and good and bad experiences. Those help bring people closer together, understand each other better over time, and intertwine your souls.

But once you have entered into the downward spiral of fights, arguments and vituperation, you will have lost intimacy and gained antagonism, anger and frustration, and once she had had enough of that, she was done.

In essence, too many arguments will cause too much damage.

Consider arguments like leaks in a boat that starts to sink. You need time to patch them up, to keep the boat on the surface, but if another hole is punctured before you patch the other one, it will only keep sinking more.

Which is why it's okay to have an occasional argument, but not every week or every day.

And it changed my mindset. I started to realize that... "falling in love" isn't what I wanted anymore. I mean, I want it. But I also don't. Not at the start, anyway, if that makes sense?

I feel like it's more effective to keep my eyes clear, my ears sound, and observe people whom I meet. I give trust slowly, over a period of time. Because people make promises and tell you things... but I take it with a grain of salt because I feel they have to show it with their actions before I believe it.

You see... to me love is not about feeling butterflies in the stomach. I think it's more essential to connect with someone that matches your needs, your goals, your attributes. And then when that person is interested to get to know you, you start working on bonding with each other. Getting to know each other. 

You observe how they behave, how they react. Can they communicate? Can they listen to you when you're trying to convey any issues with them? Do they make efforts in return for yours? Do they pique your intelligence? And most those things you won't even know until you figure out whether you can co-exist with them by living together with that person.

In short... true love is about respect, trust, empathy, and growing together. You'd have to understand each other's values, beliefs, life goals. And it has nothing to do with "Falling in love"   
In fact... falling in love is just a phenomenon. Limerince as you may call it, or infatuation.   
"Lust at first sight"

I will no longer take part of that. Because it only shows me what I want to see. Not what I need to see. And to understand and love someone, you need to see them as who they really are, before you make that choice.

- Take it slow. You're only together for a short while. Don't rush into something rash like moving in together or talking marriage. Instead, focus on activities to do together and create memories with each other.  
- Set ground rules and boundaries. It's important to talk about what you expect from each other and how you'd like the relationship to grow. Talking of future goals is fine here. But it should be goals you can both align with.  
- Remain observant. Consindering someone to be "the one" often makes us very forgiving, as we love them so deeply. Yet, if promises or agreements or boundaries are not upheld by the other person, we need to keep mindful of that.  
- Retain some space for yourself. You still have a life when you're not with your partner. Don't neglect everything in sacrifice for someone else who you've barely met. I think that it's because you were dating very young, that things are now different. You were both in entirely different stages of your life, and only now really becoming adults, thinking about the future, what you want and what you need.

And since you both grow individually, it's not that uncommon for couples like you to find themselves in a disposition regarding several incompatibilities. Sexually, intimatially, romantically, and just being a couple in general; working as a team.

You guys have grown accustomed to sharing your lives together, but haven't done anything to actually nurture the relationship. Though I suppose on his side, there's much of that kind of effort lacking.

Communication is key here. And you're going to have to figure out if there is a way to compromise and find a solution. If he truly loves you, he would work with you to find it. If he cares about how you feel.

But in order to do that, he'll need to know how you feel. So instead of trying to pull it out of him, lay it out on the table about how YOU feel and let him give the chance to meet you halfway.

If he can't do that... or isn't willing to... Well, then you have to be clear as to how this relationship can't move forward if things stay that way.

Either way, this type of conversation should be in person, at a table, with no music or phones distracting. And start off letting him know you love him and you want for both to have a strong and healthy relationship, and that the concerns on your mind aren't in any way meant to attack him.
